titles.202: Annotatio III §.II open: More perfect Consociation attempt owed to Bucer — vies with Melanchthon for palm of theological moderation; still presses Concord after Marburg
titles.203: Annotatio III §.II: Bucer to Luther at Coburg, then to Oecolampadius and Zwingli — delays stretch to the sixth year; Concord finally set at Wittenberg
titles.204: Annotatio III §.II: Second Consociation attempt ranked WITTENBERGENSE — Formula explains Coena consensus; eleven Reformed and six Lutheran subscribers; almost Interim-like pending wider approval
titles.205: Annotatio III §.II: From the Lutheran side — Luther himself urges Bucer toward Concord (1535); then presses Strasbourg and Swiss approvals (1536–1538)
titles.206: Annotatio III §.II: From the Reformed side — Wittenberg Formula never revoked, only declared; Helvetian approval; Zurich reply dated 4 May 1538 (not 1539 typo in Werenfels)
titles.207: Annotatio III §.II: Zurich reply (German) — joy at Luther’s answer; Capito and Bucer’s report; Basel Confession accepted; unity on Word, Baptism, and Supper without empty signs — Hucusque Tigurini
titles.208: Annotatio III §.II close: Werenfels votes to renew the short-lived 1536 Concord; Luther’s 1 Dec 1537 letter; Strimesius joins the wish — Concord later ruptured; Luther’s bitter Jan 1546 letter before death on the Feast of Concord — stop before §.III Francofurtanum

latin.202:
§. II.
Sequitur perfectius Consociationis Molimen, Martino Bucero, vel cum placidissimo Melanchthone de palma moderationis modestiaeque Theologicae certaturo, debitum, hisce Chytraei verbis praecedenti Molimini attextum: Cùm autem, inquit, Landgravius Intercessione obtinere non potuisset, ut Zwingliani in Fratrum numerum à Saxonibus recepti admitterentur, tamen post exhibitam quoque à Nostris Confessionem, Bucerus non destitit, ineundae Conciliationis & Concordiae rationes omni curâ & studio urgere, pag. 658. Et pag. 679.
latin.203: Nihilominus Bucerus pautò post, ante Comitiorum exitum, praesciente Electore Saxoniae & suo Magistratu, ad Lutherum, Coburgam profectus est, ut de piis rationibus & mediis componendae hujus Controversiae, cum eo transigeret; eâdem de causa aliquanto post ad Oecolampadium & Zwinglium se contulit. Sed variis subinde intervenientibus remoris, actionis illius conclusio in sextum usque annum dilata & Wittenbergae tandem Concordia constituta est.
latin.204: Perfectius eo nomine reputandum duco Molimen hoc Consociationis Secundum, WITTENBERGENSE, ob Formulam Concordiae Wittenbergensem, etiam Consensum in Dogmate de Coena explicantem, ab undecim Reformatae, & sex Lutheranae partis Theologis subscriptam, legendamque apud Chytraeum pag. 680. 681.; Utut Interimisticum quasi dicendum, quòd Concordiam illam (sunt verba Chytraei) non concludere omninò voluerint dicti Theologi, priusquam ad caeteros etiam Theologos & Magistratus, eam, ceu ab his quoque approbandam, retulissent.
latin.205: Accedit ad Perfectionem Concordiae Wittenbergensis à parte LUTHERANORUM, Bucerum ad hanc Concordiam quaerendam, à Luthero ipso incitatum fuisse, Literis ad Argentinenses datis, Anno 1535. apud Buddeum Epist. 120. pag. 248.; Post Formulam Concordiae constitutam, approbationem Argentinensium Anno 1536. Lutherum ursisse, Epistola 223. pag. 257. etiam Helvetiorum Anno 1537. 1. Decembr. Epist. 231 & Anno 1538. Epist. 232.
latin.206: A PARTE REFORMATORUM Formulam Concordiae Wittenbergensem nunquam fuisse revocatam, sed declaratam duntaxat vid. Crocium, Comment. August. Confess. pag. 162. sigillatim ab Helvetiis approbatam, Croc. pag. 100. & 107. cujus approbationis, quippe à nonnullis in dubium vocatae, non possumus non testes Helvetiorum advocare responsorias paulò licèt seriùs Tiguro, ad Lutherum datas; non tamen Annô demum 1539. cui anno, fortè per errorem typographicum, assignatas eas invenio in parte Concionis Werenfelsianae, hôc ipsô, quô haec scribo, annô, Berolini typis exscripta, sed exaratas Anno 1538, die 4. Maji, adeoque dimidio circiter post anno à reddita sibi Lutheri Epistola, uti memorant Historiae Augustanae Confess. Scriptores tres Lutheranorum celebratissimi, Selneccerus, Kirchnerus & Chemnitius, dictas literas verbis sequentibus recensentes:
latin.207: Ehrwürdiger Hochgelahrter in Christo / w. sonders geliebter Herr und Freund / wir haben euere freundliche und gutherzige Antwort / die ihr uns auf das Schreiben / welches wir euch gen Schmalkalden gethan / verschienen Tagen zugesandt / mit höchster Freud und Frolocken zu GOtt unserm himlischen Vater / empfangen / ... Und dieweil wir den nicht allein aus eurem Schreiben / sondern auch der hochgelehrten unserer insonders geliebten Herrn / Freunde und Brüdern / D. Capitonis und Buceri ... nicht anders verstehen können / denn das ihr den Handel dieser heiligen Einigkeit wol und gut meinet / ... desgleichen auch unser zu Basel gestellete Confeßion / zu sampt der darauff gefolgten Declaration ... zu gutem gefallen annemet / ... Dieweil wir auch der Artickel halben vom eufferlichen Wort und Tauffe / sehen / das E.E. keinen Misverstand findet / ... und daneben bey dem Artickel des heiligen Sacraments des Leibs und Bluts Christi verstanden / das ihr noch nie gelehret habt / auch noch nicht lehret / daß Christus vom Himmel / von der rechten Hand Gottes seines Vaters hernieder und auffahre ... und also keine Gegenwärtigkeit / oder Niessung des Leibes und Bluts Christi im heiligen Abendmahl setzet / aus der etwas folgete / das der wahren Menschwerdung und Himmelfahrt Christi ... wiedrig ... wir auch dagegen nicht wollen / das im Abendmahl allein blosse oder leere zeichen / sondern auch der Leib und das Blut des HErrn empfangen und genossen werde / also / das dis an ihm selbst allein durch das gläubige Gemuth warlich begriffen und empfangen werde / ... so können wir numehr nicht anders sehen noch befinden / denn das wir / (Gott hab Lob) im Verstande und rechter substanz mit einander einig / und zu gutem Frieden / auch kein Streit mehr zwischen uns sey ... Pag. integra Hh / Hucusque verba Tigurinorum,
latin.208:
quibus B. Werenfelsius, Theologiae Professor quondam Primarius Basiliensis, permotus videtur, in dicta Concione, Votô sequenti defungi, subjectâ praeterea Epistola Lutheri, quae paulò antè recensitas Tigurinorum responsorias elicuerunt: Ware wol zu wünschen / daß diß in acht genommen / und die / bald nach der Reformation Anno 1536. / zwischen den Evangelischen Theologis beyder Theilen / gemachte / aber leyder nicht mehr als 3. Jahr warende Concordi oder Einigkeit / wieder erneuert würde / von deren Doctor Luther an die Evangelischen Eidgenossen also geschrieben: Bitte demühtig / wollet euch zu mir versehen / als zu einem / der es ja auch von Herzen meinet / und was zur Förderung der Concordi dienet / so viel nur immer möglich / an mir nichts mangeln soll ... Der Brieff ist datirt den 1. Decembr. Anno 1537. Operum Lutheri Tom. 6. Jenensi f. 507.
Voto Werenfelsiano & nostrum jungimus, tantò ferventiùs, quantò, proh dolor certius est, ob causas mere carnales, B. Calixto Seniori Jud. Controv. Num. 72. & 75. memoratas, Concordiam Wittenbergensem à Luthero priori ruptam fuisse, quin Lutherum (quod tamen saltem citra intentionem scientiamque ejus evenisse speramus) Schismati immortuum videri posse per Epistolam suam ad Jacobum Praepositum mense, antequàm è vivis die 18. Februarii Concordiae sacrô, excessisset, hisce verbis conceptam: ... Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio Sacramentariorum, nec stetit in via Zwinglianorum, nec sedet in cathedra Tigurinorum. Habes quid sentiam. ... 17. Jan. 1546. Clariss. Buddeus Supplem. Epistol. Lutheri, Epist. 255. pag. 287. 288.

pass_a.202: §. II. There follows a more perfect Consociation Effort, owed to Martin Bucer — who was about to contend even with the most placid Melanchthon for the palm of theological moderation and modesty — attached to the preceding Effort in these words of Chytraeus: When however, he says, the Landgrave by Intercession could not obtain that the Zwinglians be admitted, received into the number of Brothers by the Saxons, nevertheless after Our Confession had also been exhibited, Bucer did not desist from urging with all care and zeal the reasons/means of entering Conciliation and Concord, p. 658. And p. 679.
pass_a.203: Nevertheless Bucer a little later, before the exit of the Diets, with the Elector of Saxony and his own Magistrate knowing beforehand, set out to Luther at Coburg, so that he might treat with him about pious reasons and means of composing this Controversy; for the same cause somewhat later he betook himself to Oecolampadius and Zwingli. But with various delays intervening one after another, the conclusion of that action was deferred all the way to the sixth year, and at Wittenberg at last Concord was established.
pass_a.204: For that reason I judge this Second Consociation Effort more perfect, the WITTENBERG one, on account of the Wittenberg Formula of Concord, which also explains the Consensus in the Dogma concerning the Supper, subscribed by eleven theologians of the Reformed party and six of the Lutheran, and to be read in Chytraeus pp. 680–681; even if it is almost to be called Interim-like, because those theologians (Chytraeus’s words) did not want to conclude that Concord altogether before they had also referred it to the remaining Theologians and Magistrates, as something to be approved by them as well.
pass_a.205: There is added to the Perfection of the Wittenberg Concord from the LUTHERAN side, that Bucer was spurred by Luther himself toward seeking this Concord, by Letters given to the Strasburgers, in the Year 1535, in Buddeus Epistle 120, p. 248; After the Formula of Concord was established, Luther pressed the approval of the Strasburgers in the Year 1536, Epistle 223, p. 257, and also of the Helvetians in the Year 1537, December 1, Epistle 231, and in the Year 1538, Epistle 232.
pass_a.206: FROM THE REFORMERS’ SIDE, that the Wittenberg Formula of Concord was never revoked, but only declared — see Crocius, Commentary on the Augsburg Confession, p. 162; approved seal-by-seal by the Helvetians, Crocius pp. 100 and 107; of which approval, inasmuch as it has been called into doubt by some, we cannot but summon as witnesses the Helvetians’ reply-letters given a little later from Zurich to Luther; yet not only in the Year 1539 at last — to which year, perhaps by typographical error, I find them assigned in a part of the Werenfelsian Sermon printed at Berlin in this very year in which I write — but written in the Year 1538, on the 4th day of May, and so about half a year after Luther’s Epistle had been returned to them, as the three most celebrated Lutheran writers of the History of the Augsburg Confession — Selneccer, Kirchner, and Chemnitz — recount, reviewing the said letters in the following words:
pass_a.207: Honorable, highly learned in Christ, especially beloved Lord and Friend: we have received your friendly and kind-hearted Answer — which you sent us in recent days to the Writing we made to you toward Schmalkalden — with highest joy and rejoicing to God our heavenly Father ... And since we can understand not otherwise, not only from your Writing but also from the faithful opening and report of our especially beloved Lords, Friends and Brothers, Dr. Capito and Bucer, who were with us that day, than that you mean well and good the business of this holy Unity ... and likewise that you take in good pleasure our Confession drawn up at Basel together with the Declaration that followed on it ... Since also concerning the Articles of the outward Word and Baptism we see that Your Honor finds no misunderstanding ... and beside that, on the Article of the holy Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ, we understand that you have never taught, and still do not teach, that Christ comes down and goes up from heaven, from the right hand of God his Father ... and so you set no Presence or eating of Christ’s Body and Blood in the holy Supper from which something would follow contrary to the true Incarnation and Ascension of Christ ... we also on the other side do not want that in the Supper only bare or empty signs, but also the Body and Blood of the Lord, be received and enjoyed — so that this in itself is truly grasped and received only through the believing mind ... therefore we can now see and find nothing else than that we (God have praise) are one with each other in understanding and right substance, and unto good peace, and that there is no more dispute between us ... Full page Hh / Thus far the words of the Zurichers,
pass_a.208: by which words Blessed Werenfels, once Primary Professor of Theology at Basel, seems moved, in the said Sermon, to discharge himself with the following Vote, with Luther’s Epistle also subjoined which a little earlier elicited the Zurichers’ replies just reviewed: It were much to be wished that this were taken to heart, and that the Concord or Unity made soon after the Reformation in the Year 1536 between the Evangelical Theologians of both sides — but alas lasting no more than 3 years — would be renewed again, of which Doctor Luther wrote thus to the Evangelical Swiss Confederates: I ask humbly that you would take me for one who means it from the heart, and that whatever serves the furthering of Concord, so far as ever possible, nothing shall be lacking in me ... The Letter is dated 1 December, Year 1537. Luther’s Works, Jena Tom. 6, f. 507. To Werenfels’s Vote we also join ours, so much the more fervently as — alas — it is more certain that, for merely carnal causes recounted by Blessed Calixtus the Elder, Jud. Controv. Nos. 72 and 75, the Wittenberg Concord was ruptured by the earlier Luther, nay that Luther (which yet we hope happened at least beside his intention and knowledge) can seem to have died into the Schism, by his Epistle to Jakob Praepositus in the month before he departed from the living on the 18th of February, the sacred day of Concord, conceived in these words: ... Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the Sacramentarians, nor stood in the way of the Zwinglians, nor sits in the chair of the Zurichers. You have what I think. ... 17 Jan. 1546. The most illustrious Buddeus, Supplement of Luther’s Epistles, Epistle 255, pp. 287–288.

202: §. II. Next comes a more complete Consociation attempt — one owed to Martin Bucer, who could even vie with the gentlest Melanchthon for the palm of theological moderation and modesty.

Chytraeus tacks it onto the Marburg effort in these words: when the Landgrave’s intercession could not get the Saxons to receive the Zwinglians as brothers, Bucer still did not quit — even after our Confession had been shown — but kept pressing every path to conciliation and Concord (pp. 658 and 679).
203: Still, a little later — before the diets closed, and with the Elector of Saxony and Bucer’s own magistrates knowing — Bucer went to Luther at Coburg to work out godly ways of settling the controversy.
For the same cause he soon went on to Oecolampadius and Zwingli.
One delay after another pushed the close of that business out to the sixth year; Concord was finally constituted at Wittenberg.
204: On that account I rank this second Consociation attempt higher — the Wittenberg one — because of the Wittenberg Formula of Concord, which even spells out agreement on the doctrine of the Supper.
Eleven Reformed and six Lutheran theologians subscribed it; read it in Chytraeus, pp. 680–681.

Call it almost Interim-like if you like: those theologians (Chytraeus’s words) would not finish the Concord until they had also referred it to the other theologians and magistrates for their approval.
205: From the Lutheran side, another mark of the Wittenberg Concord’s completeness is this: Luther himself spurred Bucer to seek it — letters to the Strasburgers, 1535 (Buddeus, Epistle 120, p. 248).
After the Formula was set, Luther pressed Strasbourg’s approval in 1536 (Epistle 223, p. 257), and the Swiss as well — 1 December 1537 (Epistle 231) and 1538 (Epistle 232).
206: From the Reformed side: the Wittenberg Formula of Concord was never revoked — only declared (Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 162).
The Swiss approved it point by point (Crocius, pp. 100 and 107).

Because some have doubted that approval, we must call the Helvetians’ own reply letters from Zurich to Luther as witnesses — written a little later, yet not as late as 1539 (the year a Berlin printing of Werenfels’s sermon assigns them, perhaps by typographical error, in this very year of my writing).

They were drawn up on 4 May 1538 — about half a year after Luther’s letter reached them — as Selneccer, Kirchner, and Chemnitz, the three most celebrated Lutheran historians of the Augsburg Confession, recount when they cite the letters in these words:
207: The Zurich letter opens: Honorable, highly learned friend in Christ — we received with highest joy your kind answer to the writing we sent you toward Schmalkalden, thanking our heavenly Father.

From your letter and from Capito and Bucer’s faithful report while they were with us, we can only take it that you mean this holy unity well, and that you gladly accept our Basel Confession with the Declaration that followed.

On the outward Word and Baptism you find no misunderstanding; on the holy Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood we gather you have never taught — and do not teach — a descent or ascent from the Father’s right hand that would set a presence or eating in the Supper contrary to the true incarnation and ascension.

We for our part refuse bare empty signs in the Supper: the Lord’s body and blood are received, yet truly grasped only by the believing mind, as our Confession and Declaration sent to Schmalkalden still hold.
So we now see nothing else than that — God be praised — we are one in understanding and right substance, at peace, with no dispute left between us. (Full page Hh.) Thus far the Zurichers’ words.
208: Those Zurich words seem to move Werenfels — once chief theology professor at Basel — to end his sermon with this wish, adding the Luther letter that had drawn the Zurich replies: would that the Concord made in 1536 between the evangelical theologians of both sides — alas lasting no more than three years — were renewed.

Of that Concord Luther wrote to the evangelical Swiss on 1 December 1537 (Jena Works, Tom. 6, f. 507): take me for one who means it from the heart; so far as I can, nothing that furthers Concord shall be lacking in me.

We join Werenfels’s wish — the more warmly because, alas, it is surer still that for merely carnal causes (Calixtus the Elder, Jud. Controv. nos. 72 and 75) the earlier Luther broke the Wittenberg Concord.

Worse: by his letter to Jakob Praepositus in the month before he died — 18 February, the holy day of Concord — Luther can seem to have died into the schism (we hope at least beside his intention and knowledge): Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the Sacramentarians, nor stood in the way of the Zwinglians, nor sits in the chair of the Zurichers. You have what I think. (17 January 1546; Buddeus, Supplement, Epistle 255, pp. 287–288.)
Stop before §. III — the third, Frankfurt attempt after Luther’s death.
